{"id": "7:12/q14", "question": "What do reports say about the creation of angels, Iblis and Adam?", "turns_on": "The transmitted wording and attributed source of each creation report.", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q14/p1", "position": "A report from ʿAʾisha says angels were made from light, Iblis or jinn from fire, and Adam as described in the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim's version for angels, Iblis and Adam; Ibn Mardawayh's variant has light of the Throne and jinn. A wording outside the sound collection adds houris from saffron. Ibn Ashur cites the report in discussing whether jinn differ from angels."}, {"id": "7:12/q14/p2", "position": "Abu Salih says Iblis came from the fire of might and angels from the light of might.", "reasons": "Durr reports this distinct provenance."}]}
{"id": "7:12/q15", "question": "What does this verse say about the origin and limits of analogy in religion?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported censure is universal or specifically about mistaken, self-directed analogy.", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q15/p1", "position": "Iblis was the first to reason by analogy or personal religious opinion and erred.", "reasons": "Hasan, Ibn Sirin and Ibn Abbas are reported repeatedly; Ibn Sirin also says sun and moon worship came by analogy. Thaʿlabi and others transmit Ibn Abbas's warning that self-directed religious analogizers are joined with Iblis. Ibn Kathir calls Ibn Jarir's chains for Hasan and Ibn Sirin sound. Durr and Tabatabai transmit prophetic versions, and Jaʿfar says followers of such opinion join Iblis at resurrection."}, {"id": "7:12/q15/p2", "position": "The first-analogy reports target corrupt reasoning, not all principled inference.", "reasons": "Tabari reads Hasan and Ibn Sirin as condemning erroneous analogy; Ibn Atiyya says their words warned of Khārijite and other false analogies, not a blanket rejection. Wahidi says Ibn Abbas warns against personal opinion."}]}
{"id": "7:12/q16", "question": "When is legal analogy valid in light of Iblis's example?", "turns_on": "Whether analogy is being used against a governing command, has legal foundations, and can restrict a general text.", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q16/p1", "position": "Grounded analogy is valid or required where no text governs; analogy opposing text is invalid.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and Study Quran distinguish Iblis's opposition to command from scholarly inference. Qurtubi cites majority acceptance, Bukhari's sequence of scripture, Sunna, consensus then analogy, Tabari's binding duty of inference, consensus claimed by Abu Tammam, and examples: Ali's imamate and wine-penalty analogies, Abu Bakr on zakat and prayer, Umar's instruction to Abu Musa and reasoning about plague. Qaffal and Abu al-Husayn al-Basri call analogy rationally obligatory. Qurtubi calls baseless conjecture prohibited by 17:36."}, {"id": "7:12/q16/p2", "position": "Analogy is rationally and legally impossible or generally rejected.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports Nazzam and some literalists; Study Quran notes Jaʿfarī rejection and that Hanbalis usually oppose or rarely use qiyās. Ibn Abbas's and Jaʿfar's reports are invoked against it."}, {"id": "7:12/q16/p3", "position": "A general scriptural command cannot be narrowed by analogy.", "reasons": "Razi reports opponents of specification: Iblis's fire-clay comparison exempted him from a command including him, and the severe blame condemns that move. Alusi reports the rival view that he accepted the command and objected to its wisdom; he says exemption may instead nullify the text outright."}]}
{"id": "7:12/q17", "question": "What wider moral pattern does Iblis's answer reveal?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q17/p1", "position": "Self-assertion and judging by lineage or matter conceal dependence on God.", "reasons": "Sulami's Wasiti says even the bare 'I' would ruin him; Qushayri says rank is God's gift. Bursevi's poems warn against outward appearance and analogy before certainty. Elmalili says learned material reduction repeats Iblis's error; Islahi calls lineage-based superiority satanic."}, {"id": "7:12/q17/p2", "position": "The contrast with Adam shows refusal versus confession, repentance and hope.", "reasons": "Zajjaj contrasts Iblis's persisted defiance with Adam and Eve in 7:23; Study Quran says Iblis seeks revenge while Adam accepts guilt; Tabari and Qaffal attribute the outcomes to their different tendencies under divine decree."}]}
{"id": "7:12/q18", "question": "How is this dialogue related to other tellings and to the sūra?", "turns_on": "Whether differences among the accounts carry rhetorical force and how this scene serves the sūra.", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q18/p1", "position": "Al-Aʿraf's shorter, stronger wording conveys greater divine displeasure than Ṣād's fuller exchange.", "reasons": "Samarrai compares omission of Iblis's name, added emphatic lā and explicit command here with Ṣād's named address and 'two hands'; Ṣād adds fa, 'Lord' and a set time to the respite exchange. Aʿraf's story has more emphatic forms and nine prostration derivatives versus Ṣād's three; its ending has angels prostrating. Its opening letters, especially alif and lām, suit the added lā; earlier scholars noted sūra-wide letter patterns and Jaʿfar counted alif-lām-rāʾ 220 times in its sūra. Burhan records the presence of lā in Aʿraf and Hijr but absence in Ṣād. Ibn Ashur cross-refers to the Aaron question in 20:92–93."}, {"id": "7:12/q18/p2", "position": "The episode prepares the sūra's warning about Satan's lasting hostility and temptation.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur links it to 7:27 and shirk; Islahi traces hostility to jealousy over preference for Adam and the challenge Satan seeks to prove."}, {"id": "7:12/q18/p3", "position": "The repeated 'he said' carries the dialogue forward and marks a shift of address.", "reasons": "Alusi says the first resumes the story after an implied question and the second introduces Iblis's reply; Ibn Ashur calls the shift from 'We said' to 'He said' iltifāt."}, {"id": "7:12/q18/p4", "position": "The narrative states real relations and a disobeyable command.", "reasons": "Tabatabai rejects treating the prostration and tree commands as creative or ontological, because such commands cannot be disobeyed; he records the objection distinguishing creative from legislative command."}, {"id": "7:12/q18/p5", "position": "The parallel verses confirm Iblis's fire claim without endorsing his claim of merit.", "reasons": "Study Quran points to 15:33 and 38:76; Asad points to his note at 38:76; Tabatabai cites 18:50, 15:26–27 and 55:14–15 while stressing God's choice of Adam."}]}
{"id": "7:12/q19", "question": "What ancillary language and narrative notes accompany the source set?", "turns_on": "These supplied rows concern separate examples or general principles alongside the verse notes.", "positions": [{"id": "7:12/q19/p1", "position": "Sibawayh surveys derivational patterns for ailments, emotions, qualities and related adjectives.", "reasons": "He groups faʿila/yafʿalu with faʿal and faʿil, alternatives faʿīl and faʿlān, semantic extensions from bodily affliction to fear, sorrow, defects and agitation, and afʿala pairings. Abū al-Khaṭṭāb equates ahyam and haymān. He also notes min omitted after fear verbs. These notes concern other lexical examples."}, {"id": "7:12/q19/p2", "position": "Sibawayh surveys verbs with one or two objects and limited omission of prepositions.", "reasons": "He uses 7:155 for ikhtāra, distinguishes naming from calling, and cites poetry by Farazdaq, ʿAmr b. Maʿdīkarib, Mutalammis and an unnamed poet. He notes that not all verbs permit omitted prepositions or extra objects."}, {"id": "7:12/q19/p3", "position": "Jurjani distinguishes verb-focused from object-focused negation and their compatible contrasts.", "reasons": "He contrasts 'mā ḍarabtu Zaydan' with 'mā Zaydan ḍarabtu'; fronted 'I' plus illā conflicts with the asserted exception. Object-fronting presupposes an act but changes its object."}, {"id": "7:12/q19/p4", "position": "The Kashshaf excerpts discuss Pharaoh, Moses and Israel in 7:127–129.", "reasons": "They parse wa-yadharaka as coordinated, responsive, accusative with implicit an, nominative, jussive, or Anas's nūn reading; discuss wa-ilāhatika, Pharaoh's idols and renewed killing, Moses' reassurance, inheritance of Egypt or earth, the good end, Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud's accusative, and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd's application to al-Manṣūr."}, {"id": "7:12/q19/p5", "position": "Other side notes give general language or usage observations.", "reasons": "Majaz introduces concise expression without repeating material, though the excerpt stops before its example; Burhan gives a general rule for blame in divine questions and for ellipsis; Ibn Kathir glosses ablasa as despair of mercy; Samarrai corrects an apology construction."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q01", "question": "How is Adam's address connected to the preceding speech?", "turns_on": "Whether the wāw continues the expulsion speech or introduces an understood new saying, with 2:35 supplying that wording.", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q01/p1", "position": "An unspoken divine saying introduces the address.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī supplies 'And We said'; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī infer it from 2:35. Al-Ālūsī favors connection to the earlier angelic command and favors to humanity; the direct call gives the command weight. Al-Kashshāf simply expands the call as God's address to Adam."}, {"id": "7:19/q01/p2", "position": "The address continues the same quoted speech as Iblis's expulsion.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says wāw joins the speech of 7:18 and the speaker turns to Adam without repeating 'We said'; his prophetic legal-case example and 12:28–29 illustrate successive addressees. This juxtaposition humiliates Iblis and honors Adam. Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts this shared saying with the explicit 'We said' in 2:35. Al-Ālūsī reports an argument for this connection but finds it agai

{"id": "7:19/q02", "question": "What does the call to Adam convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q02/p1", "position": "It draws attention to Adam and honors him.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says direct address makes the command important and singles out Adam's priority; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the vocative honors him before the gathered company and sharpens Iblis's humiliation. Study Quran contrasts this intimate direct address with God's later call from a distance, signaling alienation."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q03", "question": "What does the command to dwell mean for Adam?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q03/p1", "position": "Take up or continue residence in the Garden.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Nasafī distinguish residence from mere stillness; al-Ālūsī explicitly rejects the sense of immobility. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says a command to continue an existing action means persistence. Ibn ʿĀshūr says if Adam was created there it means remain, and if elsewhere it grants entry as an honor; either taunts Iblis. Al-Bursevī adds that the residence honors the pair and permits their stay."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q04", "question": "Why is the independent pronoun 'you' stated?", "turns_on": "Whether coordination requires both nouns to be independently eligible for the same verb form.", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q04/p1", "position": "It reinforces Adam as the subject and enables coordination with his wife.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj prefers the pronoun because 'go and Zayd' without one is awkward. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the hidden subject of 'dwell' particularly needs reinforcement; al-Burhān says a connected subject is conventionally reinforced before a coordinated noun. Al-Biqāʿī adds that it confirms Adam himself, rather than a metonymic associate, is addressed. Ibn ʿĀshūr sees an indirect contrast with Iblis, applicable also to 2:35, while denying that pronouns inherently carry contrast."}, {"id": "7:19/q04/p2", "position": "The wife's mention represents a separate, omitted command to dwell.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmarūn and Ibn Mālik require both coordinated nouns to be eligible for the same grammatical role. Abū Ḥayyān counters with 'Hind and Zayd rise': masculine Zayd may be coordinated after a feminine verb although he could not independently be its subject."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q05", "question": "Who is Adam's spouse, and what is reported of her origin?", "turns_on": "The reported account of Eve's origin: formed from Adam or already among the Garden's women.", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q05/p1", "position": "She is Eve, created from Adam.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, al-Jishumī, al-Bursevī, and Study Quran identify her as Ḥawwāʾ/Eve; Study Quran notes the Quran never names her. Al-Suddī reports that Adam awoke to a companion made from his rib, named Ḥawwāʾ because she came from living matter. Study Quran says the rib account appears in Hadith and many read 4:1 as alluding to her origin; it notes that the Quran omits the origin and that primordial Adam represents male and female humanity. Kuranyolu says Adam was made on earth from special soil and his mate from him."}, {"id": "7:19/q05/p2", "position": "Ḥawwāʾ was one of the Garden's women.", "reasons": "Ashʿath al-Ḥaddānī adds that her pregnancy was so transparent the child's sex could be seen."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q06", "question": "Why is the wife described as Adam's 'zawj'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q06/p1", "position": "The expression concisely conveys their paired relationship and shared address.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevī says zawj names one counterpart and zawjān the pair. Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī say the possessive relation makes a feminine form redundant. Al-Ālūsī says Eve follows Adam in the residence command, whereas both are addressed equally in eating and prohibition; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī likewise says the ruling includes her though Adam alone is directly addressed. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes that the Quran also uses zauj for Adam's spouse in the parallel addresses at 2:35 and 20:117."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q07", "question": "Which Garden did Adam and his wife inhabit?", "turns_on": "Whether the setting is final recompense, another heavenly test garden, an earthly garden, or specifically Eden; accounts weigh departure, prohibition, sleep, and Iblis's presence differently.", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q07/p1", "position": "The Garden of Eternity or final reward.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says leaving it was possible because their stay was not permanent reward; al-Jishumī attributes the choice to ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā. Al-Bursevī calls this the majority view. Kuranyolu prefers it after considering parallel verses: the pair were created on earth, then placed in a Paradise unlike earthly life."}, {"id": "7:19/q07/p2", "position": "A heavenly garden distinct from the final Garden.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī attributes a heavenly-gardens view to Abū ʿAlī and Abū Hāshim. Al-Bursevī reports a test garden in heaven as one alternative; its advocates cite prohibitions, sleep, expulsion, and Iblis's entry as unlike eternal reward. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī specifies an intermediate heavenly garden before earthly life and legal responsibility, revealing general human disposition."}, {"id": "7:19/q07/p3", "position": "An earthly garden.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports an earthly garden without duties, although Adam was obligated. Al-Bursevī prefers earth: a report says Adam's sons sought Garden grapes at his death and angels buried him; he also interprets the Nile's Garden source as earthly. Kuranyolu gives the lexical earthly-garden view. Other test-garden advocates mention an earthly elevated garden and objections to identifying the site with final reward."}, {"id": "7:19/q07/p4", "position": "The Garden of Eden, distinct from Eternity.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the place of Adam and expelled Iblis as Eden. Elmalılı glosses adn with unvowelled dāl as residence, linked to maʿdin, and suggests Eden was the first afterlife garden on the way to Eternity, where beginning and return meet, citing 43:72."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q08", "question": "When were Adam and his wife settled in the Garden?", "turns_on": "Different reports supply relative sequence and a specific day; the details are not mutually exclusive.", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q08/p1", "position": "After Iblis was expelled; Adam had previously been alone there.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, and al-Bursevī place the divine address after Iblis's expulsion. Al-Suddī says Adam first lived alone, then awoke to his wife."}, {"id": "7:19/q08/p2", "position": "Adam was created and placed in Firdaws on Friday.", "reasons": "Abū al-ʿĀliya reports both events on that day."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q09", "question": "How does 'then eat' relate to dwelling, compared with 2:35?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q09/p1", "position": "Fāʾ marks eating as following residence; 2:35's wāw gives broader conjunction.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Tafsīr al-Kabīr say succession is a special case of conjunction, resolving the variation. Al-Biqāʿī says eating accompanies settlement. Al-Itqān says taking residence comes first and min ḥaythu is narrower. Ibn ʿĀshūr says fāʾ conveys prompt, complete favor and distress to Iblis; his general principle allows Quranic variation where both formulations fit. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says wāw leaves timing and choice open while fāʾ orders eating immediately; his Lamāsāt cites 45:24, 42:3, and 5:6 to show wāw can indicate order without requiring it."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q10", "question": "How is the imperative 'eat' formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q10/p1", "position": "It comes from akala with its first root letter omitted in the imperative.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya also mentions avoidance of a difficult vowel on a weak letter."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q11", "question": "What does eating here mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q11/p1", "position": "Actual eating.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī adduces the parallel in 20:121."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q12", "question": "How far does the permission to eat extend?", "turns_on": "Whether the locution primarily ranges over places or over the fruits available there; both remain bounded by the exception.", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q12/p1", "position": "It permits broad, free use of the Garden's food, except the singled-out tree.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī mentions fruit wherever they wish; Mujāhid says no accounting for where they eat. Al-Jishumī calls it permission to enjoy blessings. Al-Ṭabrisī allows any place or manner; al-Nasafī, al-Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, al-Iṣlāḥī and Study Quran include the exception. Elmalılı insists this bounded license grants neither unlimited freedom nor ownership; the tree marks a spatial and practical limit."}, {"id": "7:19/q12/p2", "position": "It permits eating anywhere in the Garden.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī records this spatial reading as one of two ways to take the permission."}, {"id": "7:19/q12/p3", "position": "It permits eating any of the Garden's fruits.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī supports this alternative because the prohibited tree bore fruit."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q13", "question": "What is the force of 'from wherever you wish' here compared with 2:35?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q13/p1", "position": "It qualifies eating alone and is narrower than 2:35's wording.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān contrasts min ḥaythu with the broader ḥaythu shiʾtumā. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says the latter can govern both dwelling and eating, whereas this phrase governs eating only; he connects the wider Baqara wording to its honorific setting."}]}

Ibn ʿĀshūr sees favors distributed among accounts to vary narration and sustain moral instruction."}, {"id": "7:19/q14/p2", "position": "Al-Baqara's extra word suits its more honorific account; al-Aʿrāf emphasizes reproach.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī and al-Kirmānī link raghadan to al-Baqara's explicit divine 'We said' and greater honor; the al-Aʿrāf story shares the expulsion saying and later rebukes Adam. {"id": "7:19/q15", "question": "Why does al-Aʿrāf omit al-Baqara's 'from it' after eating?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q15/p1", "position": "Al-Baqara repeats the Garden reference to fit its more honorific presentation.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares the added pronoun there with its omission here."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q16", "question": "What is the force of 'do not approach' the tree?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q16/p1", "position": "Avoid it, especially eating from it; barring approach blocks the path to the forbidden act.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī glosses it as avoidance; al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ālūsī take eating to be forbidden. Al-Dāmghānī identifies lā as prohibitive; Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes the verb can be vocalized qaruba/yaqrubu."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q17", "question": "Was the tree prohibition binding, advisory, or a different kind of command?", "turns_on": "Whether the utterance legislates a duty, advises against harm, or operates ontologically; disobedience is cited against the last view.", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q17/p1", "position": "A binding prohibition and test of obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī attributes this to most; Qatāda says all creation is tested and Adam violated the trial. Al-Māwardī says the prohibition preserved knowledge and supplied a recompensable test. Elmalılı says obligation and divine limits applied even in Paradise. Al-Naḥḥās calls the wording a prohibition."}, {"id": "7:19/q17/p2", "position": "A nonbinding discouragement or guidance against self-harm.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports a nonbinding view; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says Adam was before earthly legal responsibility and the warning guided him away from harm, not violation of legislation."}, {"id": "7:19/q17/p3", "position": "An ontological command.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this view of the prostration and tree prohibition, but rejects it because ontological commands cannot be disobeyed whereas Iblis and Adam did disobey."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q18", "question": "What kind of thing can be called a 'tree'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q18/p1", "position": "Anything having a trunk.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī gives this lexical range."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q19", "question": "Which tree was forbidden?", "turns_on": "The species or special character assigned by different reports; al-Māwardī contests the colocynth report and Ibn ʿĀshūr doubts intrinsic knowledge effects.", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q19/p1", "position": "Wheat or a wheat stalk.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls it a wheat stalk; al-Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Māwardī, al-Jishumī, and Study Quran give wheat."}, {"id": "7:19/q19/p2", "position": "A grapevine.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj reports this alternative. Ibn Abī Ḥātim names Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Shaʿbī, Jaʿd ibn Hubayra, al-Suddī, and Muḥammad ibn Qays; al-Māwardī attributes it to al-Suddī. Al-Jishumī and Study Quran also report it."}, {"id": "7:19/q19/p3", "position": "A fig tree.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim attributes it to Qatāda, Mujāhid, and Ibn Jurayj; al-Māwardī gives Ibn Jurayj, and Study Quran records the species."}, {"id": "7:19/q19/p4", "position": "The tree of immortality or eternity, whose fruit angels consumed.", "reasons": "Muqātil reports angels rubbing against it for immortality; Wahb describes intertwined branches and fruit eaten by angels. Ibn Judʿān calls it the tree of eternity; Study Quran notes the Tree of Everlastingness in 20:120."}, {"id": "7:19/q19/p5", "position": "A barley tree.", "reasons": "Wahb says each grain was as large as a cow's liver, softer than butter and sweeter than honey."}, {"id": "7:19/q19/p6", "position": "A date palm.", "reasons": "Abū Mālik gives this identification."}, {"id": "7:19/q19/p7", "position": "A camphor tree.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī attributes this to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib."}, {"id": "7:19/q19/p8", "position": "The tree of knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī attributes the name to al-Kalbī; Ibn ʿĀshūr reports a Torah-like explanation that the tree intrinsically awakened knowledge of good and evil, but finds that intrinsic mechanism unlikely. Study Quran contrasts the Biblical knowledge tree with Quranic identifications."}, {"id": "7:19/q19/p9", "position": "A colocynth tree.", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq transmits it from the People of the Two Books; al-Māwardī knows no basis for the report."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q20", "question": "Why is the forbidden tree not specified by name?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q20/p1", "position": "Knowing its species would bring no benefit.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevī cites Aḥkām al-Marjān: God would have named it if doing so benefited people. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the species reports are weak and refers the question to al-Baqara; Ibn ʿAṭiyya likewise points back to his Baqara discussion."}]}
{"id": "7:19/q21", "question": "Why was this tree placed under prohibition?", "turns_on": "Whether the point lay in a moral test, a physical consequence, or a supposed intrinsic cognitive effect.", "positions": [{"id": "7:19/q21/p1", "position": "It served as a trial that set a limit amid abundant permission.", "reasons": "Qatāda says God tests all creation for obedience. Al-Māwardī says it preserved Adam's knowledge and gave an occasion for recompense. Al-Qushayrī calls spouse and tree means of ordeal within God's hidden allotment; al-Iṣlāḥī calls the one tree the pair's trial. Elmalılı says its vicinity tested their observance of limits. Ibn ʿĀshūr favors a training of resistance to appetite and developing human cognition through the first ancestor; he rejects an intrinsic knowledge-tree mechanism and compares the development with 2:31. {"id": "7:20/q15", "question": "What moral point is drawn from the exposure?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q15/p1", "position": "Unnecessary exposure of private parts is naturally shameful, even alone or before a spouse.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī calls it repugnant to instinct and reason, which Abū Ḥayyān identifies with Muʿtazilī rational moral judgment. {"id": "7:20/q16", "question": "How does 'and he said' relate to the whisper?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q16/p1", "position": "It coordinates with and explains the whisper, presenting its content.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī treat the speech as explanatory; al-Zajjāj says 7:21's oath supports direct address. {"id": "7:20/q17", "question": "What does the ban concerning this tree mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the tree is explained as an eating prohibition, sexual symbol, or deliberately unspecified.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q17/p1", "position": "God had forbidden eating from the tree; Satan falsely recast the motive as withholding angelhood or immortality.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabrisī specify eating. {"id": "7:20/q19", "question": "Why say 'this tree' with both demonstrative and noun?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q19/p1", "position": "It precisely identifies and emphasizes the particular tree.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī notes the combined demonstrative and noun."}]}

{"id": "7:20/q21", "question": "How does the exception after illā work?", "turns_on": "Whether the omitted sense is a noun of aversion, a negative particle, or a different scope for the prohibition.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q21/p1", "position": "An omitted noun supplies 'from aversion/fear that you become.'", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash compares iyyāka an tafʿala; Basrans including Sībawayh prefer an elided noun. {"id": "7:20/q22", "question": "How is malakayn read?", "turns_on": "Vocalization of the lām and the force of 20:120 as evidence.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q22/p1", "position": "With fatḥa on lām: two angels, the majority reading.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī insists on the transmitted regional reading and disallows others; Mujāhid and several readers transmit it. {"id": "7:20/q23", "question": "What sort of angelhood did the promise offer?", "turns_on": "Literal change of form, rank or innate qualities, and specific promised capacities.", "positions": [{"id": "7:20/q23/p1", "position": "A bodily change into angelic form.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports a claim that God's law permitted transformation; al-Ṭabrisī says Satan promised angelic forms. Al-Bursawī differentiates human constitution from angels' and devils' transformations."}, {"id": "7:20/q23/p2", "position": "Angelic rank, qualities, or freedom from appetite rather than changed essence.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports rank instead of form; al-Qushayrī says the pair sought freedom from desire and hope. Al-Biqāʿī notes flight and changing form; Elmalılı notes freedom from eating and drinking."}, {"id": "7:20/q23/p3", "position": "They would become angels like God or like those circling a tree branch.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās gives the 'like God' wording; Wahb describes angels circling one branch and says Satan promised that status."}, {"id": "7:20/q23/p4", "position": "Angels know good and evil, have wings, form, and honor.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan emphasizes form, wings, and honor; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Nasafī and al-Qurṭubī report knowledge of good and evil as the appeal."}, {"id": "7:20/q23/p5", "position": "The pair would live long alongside angels.", "reasons": "Abū Sulaymān al-Dimashqī gives this as one alternative to immortality without death."}]}
